title: Blackberry Jam Cake
summary: Kentucky tradition — spice cake with blackberry jam baked right in, frosted all over with caramel icing.
story: The jam goes in the batter, not between the layers — that's the Kentucky way Kelly knows. It bakes into the crumb and keeps the cake moist for days. Frost the whole thing with caramel icing and don't stop at one slice.

items: 1 cup blackberry jam (seedless if you can find it)
1 cup chopped pecans or black walnuts (optional)

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.body: Cream the butter and sugar until fluffy. Beat in the eggs one at a time, then beat in the blackberry jam — it goes right in the batter.

steps.title: Combine
steps.body: Whisk the flour, baking soda, and spices. Add to the batter alternating with the buttermilk. Fold in the nuts if using.

steps.title: Bake
steps.body: Pour into three greased 9-inch pans (or one 9x13). Bake at 350°F for 25-30 minutes, until a toothpick comes out clean. Cool completely.

steps.title: Caramel icing
steps.body: Melt the butter, stir in the brown sugar and milk, and boil 2 minutes. Cool slightly, then beat in the powdered sugar and vanilla.

steps.title: Frost
steps.body: Stack the layers and frost the whole cake all over with the caramel icing.

proTips: The jam is the flavor — use a good one, or homemade if you've got it.
The cake gets better the next day as the jam settles into the crumb.
Work fast with the caramel icing — it sets up as it cools.

title: Cowboy Beans
summary: Ground beef, bacon, and three kinds of beans in a sweet-smoky sauce. Made for the smoker.
story: Every cookout needs a pot of these. Beef, bacon, and beans go in the Dutch oven, the smoker does the rest, and the pot comes back empty.

steps.title: Brown the meat
steps.body: Brown the ground beef with the bacon, onion, and bell pepper in a cast-iron skillet or Dutch oven. Drain the grease.

steps.title: Mix it up
steps.body: Stir in everything else.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 275°F for 2 hours uncovered, stirring once halfway, until thick and bubbly. (Oven works too — 350°F for 1 hour.)

proTips: Don't skip draining the canned beans or it goes soupy.
Leftovers are even better the next day.

title: Old-Fashioned Popcorn Balls
summary: Crunchy, buttery, and just sticky enough. Tint them orange for the Halloween table.
story: Every fall needs a batch of these. Hot syrup, buttered hands, and popcorn — shaped fast before it sets.

items: 10 cups popped popcorn (about 1/2 cup kernels), unpopped kernels picked out
1 Tbsp butter, plus more for your hands

steps.title: Prep
steps.body: Put the popcorn in a big buttered bowl.

steps.title: Cook the syrup
steps.body: In a saucepan, stir the sugar, corn syrup, water, butter, and salt. Boil until it hits 250°F on a candy thermometer (hard-ball stage), about 5 minutes. Stir in the vanilla and food coloring if using.

steps.title: Coat
steps.body: Pour over the popcorn and toss fast to coat.

steps.title: Shape
steps.body: Butter your hands and shape into balls about the size of a tennis ball. Work quick — it sets fast.

steps.title: Cool
steps.body: Cool on wax paper.

proTips: Don't skip the butter on your hands or you'll be picking popcorn off your palms.
If the syrup gets too cool to shape, warm it 10 seconds in the microwave.

title: Smoke & Ember Turkey Brine
summary: The night-before soak that keeps the bird juicy through a long smoke. Salt, brown sugar, citrus, and herbs.
story: A dry turkey ruins Thanksgiving. This brine is the insurance policy — salt and sugar carry the citrus and herbs deep into the meat overnight, so the bird stays juicy no matter how long the smoke runs.

items: 1 whole garlic bulb, cut in half crosswise

steps.title: Dissolve
steps.body: In a big stockpot, heat 1/2 gallon of the water with the salt, brown sugar, peppercorns, and bay leaves. Stir until the salt and sugar dissolve, then pull it off the heat.

steps.title: Cool it down
steps.body: Add the remaining 1 1/2 gallons of cold water, the garlic, oranges, onion, thyme, and rosemary. Let it cool completely — cold to the touch, not warm.

steps.title: Submerge the bird
steps.body: Lower the turkey into the brine breast-side down. It needs to stay fully submerged — weigh it down with a plate if it floats.

steps.title: Wait
steps.body: Refrigerate 12 to 24 hours. Don't go past 24 or the meat gets hammy.

steps.title: Rinse and dry
steps.body: Pull the bird out, rinse it under cold water, and pat it completely dry with paper towels. Let it sit uncovered in the fridge for an hour so the skin dries — that's what gets you crispy skin on the smoker.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Season and smoke like normal. Skip any extra salt in your rub — the brine already handled it.

proTips: No fridge space? A brining bag in a cooler full of ice works — just keep it under 40°F.
This fits a 12 to 16 pound bird. Bigger than that, make half again as much brine.
Don't use table salt here. The iodine makes the brine taste tinny.

title: Pitmaster's Mop Sauce
summary: The thin baste that keeps long smokes juicy and builds bark. Mop it on, don't pour it.
story: The mop is the pitmaster's paintbrush. This thin vinegar mop goes on every 45 minutes once the bark sets — it keeps the meat from drying out and lays down layer after layer of flavor without washing anything off.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body: Whisk everything together in a saucepan. Bring it just to a simmer over medium heat, stirring until the sugar and salt dissolve.

steps.title: Cool & bottle
steps.body: Pull it off the heat and let it cool. Pour it into a squeeze bottle or a bowl — whatever you're mopping from.

steps.title: Mop
steps.body: Mop the meat every 45 minutes to an hour during the cook, starting after the first 2 hours. Thin coat — you're basting, not drowning it.

steps.title: Keep it warm
steps.body: Keep the mop warm on the pit or the stove while you cook. Cold mop on hot meat is a bark killer.

proTips: Don't mop in the first 2 hours. Let the bark set first or you'll wash it right off.
Built for pork butt, ribs, and brisket — anything with a long cook.
Leftover mop keeps a week in the fridge. Don't save what touched raw meat — make fresh.

title: Citrus Mojo Smoked Pork Shoulder
summary: Florida's answer to pulled pork — bright citrus, heavy garlic, Cuban soul.
story: This is what happens when a pork shoulder spends the night in citrus and garlic and then meets oak smoke. The mojo injection carries orange, lime, and garlic deep into the meat, and the long smoke turns it into the juiciest pulled pork you'll ever make.

steps.title: Mix the mojo
steps.body: Whisk the mojo together. Warm it slightly — not hot, just warm to the touch.

steps.title: Inject
steps.body: Inject the pork shoulder in a grid pattern, about an inch apart. Use all of it — this is a big piece of meat and it drinks it up.

steps.title: Rub & rest
steps.body: Coat the outside with the rub. Wrap it tight and refrigerate overnight, 8 to 12 hours.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F over oak or citrus wood until it probes tender, 200–205°F. Plan on 1.5 to 2 hours per pound.

steps.title: Rest & pull
steps.body: Rest it wrapped in a cooler for at least an hour. Pull it and spoon some of the drippings back over the meat.

proTips: Fresh citrus only — the bottled stuff tastes like cleaning product in the smoker.
This one's built for an 8 to 10 pound Boston butt.
Leftover mojo (that never touched raw meat) makes a killer dipping sauce.

title: Florida Smoked Fish Dip
summary: The dockside classic. Smoky, creamy, with a little kick — built for crackers and cold drinks.
story: Every dock in Florida has a version of this. Smoke the fish low, flake it chunky, fold it into cream cheese with lemon and heat, and let it sit overnight. By the next day it's the best thing on the table.

items: 1 lb smoked white fish (mahi, kingfish, or amberjack), flaked

steps.title: Smoke the fish
steps.body: Smoke the fish at 225°F over a mild wood (alder or apple) until it flakes easily, about 1 to 1.5 hours. Let it cool.

steps.title: Flake
steps.body: Flake the fish into a bowl, picking out any bones. Don't shred it to mush — you want some chunks in there.

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Fold in the cream cheese, mayo, sour cream, lemon juice, and hot sauce. Stir until it's combined but still chunky.

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Fold in the green onions, parsley, Old Bay, pepper, and garlic powder.

steps.title: Chill
steps.body: Cover and refrigerate at least 2 hours — overnight is better. The flavors need time to get to know each other.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Serve cold with crackers, celery, or thick-cut potato chips.

proTips: Oily fish works best — kingfish and mahi are the Florida classics, but mullet is the old-school pick.
If your fish comes out too dry from the smoker, add an extra spoonful of mayo. Nobody will know.
This keeps 4 to 5 days in the fridge. It won't last that long.

title: Key West Smoked Shrimp
summary: Pink shrimp, citrus butter, and a kiss of smoke. Done in under an hour.
story: Key West pink shrimp barely need anything — a little citrus butter, a little garlic, and a whisper of mild smoke. They cook fast, so don't walk away. Thirty minutes in the smoker and they're the best thing at the table.

items: 2 lbs large Key West pink shrimp (or Gulf shrimp), peeled and deveined, tails on
Lime wedges and fresh parsley, for serving

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Toss the shrimp with the melted butter, lime juice, garlic, Old Bay, pepper, and smoked paprika. Let it sit 15 minutes — no longer, or the lime starts cooking the shrimp.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Get the smoker to 225°F. Mild wood — alder or apple. Hickory will bully the shrimp. Lay the shrimp out on a grill pan or frog mat in a single layer.

steps.title: Cook fast
steps.body: Smoke for 30 to 45 minutes, until they're pink, firm, and curled.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Squeeze fresh lime over the top, scatter the parsley, and serve hot. Cocktail sauce optional — these don't need it.

proTips: Don't overcook them. Shrimp go from perfect to rubber in about five minutes — start checking at 30.
If you can't find Key West pinks, any Gulf shrimp works. Just don't use the tiny salad shrimp.
These are dangerous as an appetizer because nobody saves room for dinner.

title: Key West Key Lime Pie
summary: The real thing: creamy yellow, never green. Tart, sweet, and simple the way the Keys made it.
story: I've made this pie, and I'm telling you — the real Key West version is almost insultingly simple. Condensed milk, egg yolks, Key lime juice, graham cracker crust. No green food coloring, no shortcuts on the limes. The acid does all the work.

items: 1/2 cup Key lime juice (fresh Key limes, or Nellie & Joe's bottled)

steps.title: Crust
steps.body: Heat the oven to 350°F. Mix the graham cracker crumbs, sugar, and melted butter. Press it firm into a 9-inch pie dish, bottom and sides. Bake 10 minutes, then let it cool.

steps.title: Filling
steps.body: Whisk the egg yolks and condensed milk until smooth. Slowly whisk in the Key lime juice — it'll thicken up on its own. That's the magic.

steps.title: Bake
steps.body: Pour it into the cooled crust. Bake 15 minutes, until the center is just set with a slight jiggle.

steps.title: Chill
steps.body: Cool it on the counter, then refrigerate at least 3 hours — overnight is better.

steps.title: Top & serve
steps.body: Top with whipped cream and lime slices right before serving.

proTips: Real Key lime pie is yellow, not green. If it's green, something's wrong.
Don't use regular limes — Key limes or the bottled Key lime juice. Big Persian limes taste flat in this.
Sweetened condensed milk, never regular milk. That's the whole trick the sponge divers figured out.

title: Apple Pie Stuffed Pork Loin
summary: A butterflied pork loin stuffed with apple pie filling, wrapped in sweet-savory rub and finished with apple glaze.
story: Sweet meets savory in the best way. The pork loin gets butterflied, loaded with apple pie filling, rolled tight, and smoked until the glaze caramelizes on the outside. Slice it into pinwheels and watch them disappear.

steps.title: Butterfly
steps.body: Butterfly the pork loin — cut it open like a book so it lays flat, about 3/4 inch thick. Don't cut all the way through.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.body: Spread the apple pie filling down the center, leaving a 1-inch border on all sides.

steps.title: Roll & tie
steps.body: Roll it up tight from one long side and tie it with butcher's twine every 2 inches so nothing escapes.

steps.title: Rub
steps.body: Coat the whole outside with the rub. Every inch of it.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F over apple or cherry wood until it hits 145°F internal, about 2.5 to 3 hours.

steps.title: Glaze
steps.body: While it smokes, simmer the glaze ingredients until thick enough to coat a spoon, about 10 minutes. Brush it on during the last 30 minutes.

steps.title: Rest & slice
steps.body: Rest 15 minutes before slicing into pinwheels.

proTips: Tie it tight. Apple pie filling wants to escape — the twine is the only thing standing between you and a mess.
Don't skip the rest. Cut it too soon and the filling runs everywhere.
Feeds 8 to 10 off a 5-pounder.

title: Sweet Apple Glaze
summary: Apple juice, brown sugar, and cinnamon reduced into a sticky-sweet glaze. Made for pork.
story: This started as the finishing glaze for the apple pie stuffed loin, but it's too good to keep locked to one recipe. Brush it on pork chops, ribs, chicken — anything that wants a sweet apple shine.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body: Combine everything in a saucepan over medium heat. Stir until the sugar dissolves.

steps.title: Reduce
steps.body: Simmer 10 minutes, stirring now and then, until it thickens enough to coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Use
steps.body: Brush onto pork or poultry during the last 30 minutes of the cook. Keeps 2 weeks in the fridge.

proTips: Don't walk away — sugar burns fast once it starts thickening.
Warm it before brushing. Cold glaze seizes on hot meat.

title: Traditional Stuffed Pork Loin
summary: Peppers, onions, Italian sausage, and melted cheese rolled into a pork loin. The classic.
story: This is the stuffed loin I grew up on — savory all the way. Italian sausage, peppers, and onions with a core of melted cheese, rolled into a pork loin and smoked until the outside crisps and the inside goes molten.

steps.title: Cook the stuffing
steps.body: Brown the Italian sausage in a skillet, breaking it up. Add the onion, peppers, and garlic — cook until soft, about 8 minutes. Let it cool slightly.

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Mix in the mozzarella, Parmesan, parsley, and Italian seasoning.

steps.title: Butterfly
steps.body: Butterfly the pork loin — cut it open like a book so it lays flat, about 3/4 inch thick.

steps.title: Stuff & roll
steps.body: Spread the stuffing down the center, leaving a 1-inch border. Roll it up tight and tie with butcher's twine every 2 inches.

steps.title: Rub
steps.body: Coat the outside with the rub.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F over hickory or oak until it hits 145°F internal, about 2.5 to 3 hours.

steps.title: Rest & slice
steps.body: Rest 15 minutes before slicing into pinwheels.

proTips: Don't overstuff it — if the filling's spilling out before you tie it, you've got too much.
Great the next day sliced thin for sandwiches.
